article.Citation: Lawn W, et al. Well-being, problematic alcohol consumption and acute subjective drug effects in past-year ayahuasca users: a large, international, self-selecting online survey. Scientific Reports. 2017.
article.Title: Well-being, problematic alcohol consumption and acute subjective drug effects in past-year ayahuasca users: a large, international, self-selecting online survey
article.GenderCategory: male/female/transgender (whole-sample categories); Ayahuasca User subgroup: female n=146 (28.0%), male/transgender counts not broken out separately for this subgroup

ae_events.Description: Subjective rating of negative effects while high; ayahuasca rated higher than LSD/magic mushrooms (mean 3.88/10 vs 3.07/2.72), among new users
Authors attribute ayahuasca's higher negative-effects rating partly to its 'well-known vomit-inducing effects'; not separately quantified in this sample

article.IsObservational: Cross-sectional, self-selecting online drug-use survey (Global Drug Survey 2016); no randomization or research-administered intervention protocol — participants are naturalistic drug users reporting on their own prior use. Clear observational/naturalistic design.
article.Condition: Article is not an AUD-treatment study; it is a general drug-use survey that reports past-year problematic alcohol use (AUDIT scores) as a primary outcome for ayahuasca users vs. comparison groups. Coded 'Alcohol' as the closest fit among the three allowed enum values given this alcohol-outcome focus; flagged because the study population is not alcohol-use-disorder patients.
article.Substance: Ayahuasca is the substance of primary interest; LSD and magic mushrooms ('classic psychedelics') appear only as comparison/reference groups, not as a co-administered intervention, so excluded from this field.
article.N: 527 is the total 'Ayahuasca Users' (past-year use) group, the denominator used for most group-comparison analyses. Individual sub-analyses have smaller valid-case Ns due to missing data (e.g., age n=515, well-being n=521, AUDIT n=458, mental-illness n=~518) — paper explicitly reports valid percentages rather than absolute percentages where data are missing.
article.AE_denominator: No formal AE ascertainment was conducted. The only quantified negative-effect measure is the 'negative effects when high' 0-10 rating in Table 3, drawn from the subsample whose last new drug tried was ayahuasca (n=176 for that specific item, out of 191 who reported route of administration and 192 total in that subgroup).
article.ArmScope: All reported N, demographic, and effect-rating values used here are drawn exclusively from the Ayahuasca User subgroup (or the ayahuasca-first-time-try subsample), never pooled with the Classic Psychedelic or Other Respondent comparison groups.
article.PctBIPOC: Race/ethnicity not collected or reported; only country of residence, gender, and age were captured as demographic variables.
article.PctIndigenous: Not reported — no race/ethnicity data collected.
article.SafetyReported: The survey did not conduct formal clinical AE surveillance. It included a subjective 0-10 Likert item ('the negative effects while high') and a 'risk of harm following a session of use' item as part of a standard drug-effects-profile battery (also covering pleasure, strength, comedown, urge, value-for-money), plus a Discussion-section reference to ayahuasca's 'well-known vomit-inducing effects.' Coded Y because some safety-relevant signal is present, but it is a global subjective rating/background reference rather than itemized AE case reporting — flagged for reviewer judgment.
article.AnyAEReported: Negative-effects rating and vomiting are mentioned but never presented as counted/discrete AE occurrences with a participant count, so treated as 'reported but not counted.'
article.NumDistinctAEs: No countable AE types with case counts are given; only an aggregate 0-10 negative-effects rating and a qualitative mention of vomiting as a known ayahuasca effect (not quantified for this sample).
article.WorstSeverity: Both identified events (negative-effects rating, vomiting reference) are framed as expected, transient, acute-dosing phenomena with no reported intervention, hospitalization, or persistent impairment, so both default to Mild per the rubric's 'expected acute drug effects default here' rule.

ae_events.Lawn 2017_AE01: Coded AE_type='both' because the underlying survey item ('negative effects while high') is a composite rating that could reflect either physiological discomfort (AE-like) or challenging in-session psychological phenomenology (CEQ-like); article gives no further breakdown. SeverityIndeterminate='Y' because only a mean/SD group rating is available, with no description of specific symptoms, duration, or intervention — defaulted to Mild per the under-specified-AE rule in the severity rubric.
ae_events.Lawn 2017_AE02: Vomiting is named explicitly in the Discussion as a 'well-known' effect of ayahuasca used by the authors to help explain the higher negative-effects rating, but no count, proportion, or severity detail is given for this specific sample — SeverityIndeterminate='Y', defaulted to Mild absent any intervention/seriousness signal. Flagged since this is inferred from discussion-section background knowledge rather than a directly measured study finding.
